dispatch.headline: Silent Orchestra Disbands After Door Jams
dispatch.body:
Violinist Soren Glass has disbanded his orchestra. The five-piece chamber group, founded in the low-gravity domes of Grimaldi Crater, spent thirty years refining the end of their concerts. While other ensembles welcomed clapping, these musicians demanded silence.

It began simply. In 2915, they played for forty minutes and then sat perfectly still for three. By 2930, the silence lasted half an hour. The players did not rest. They leaned forward in their carbon-fibre chairs, glaring at the audience.

They watched for any movement. Glass wore magnifying lenses to track the rise and fall of listeners' chests. If a patron exhaled too loudly, the entire group stared at them until they wept. One listener, Peter Chen, was stared at for twenty minutes after his watch beeped. He left the dome.

The end came on Thursday. A letter found in Glass's instrument case revealed the secret of their famous silence. The green stage door had jammed during their first concert, and they were too embarrassed to climb over the instruments.

"We were just waiting for a technician," Glass wrote.
dispatch.scene: Soren Glass, wearing thick magnifying spectacles, leans forward from his chair on a dim stage to glare at a man in the front row.
dispatch.premise: Obituary: The Symphony of Withheld Applause, a revered lunar chamber group whose performances ended with thirty minutes of trembling, devotional silence while the orchestra openly glared at anyone who dared to exhale.

drafts.headline: Clara Sallow, Slowest Actress, Dies
drafts.body:
Madame Clara Sallow has died at her home in Grimaldi Crater. She was 102.

Born in the deep pressure of Earth, Sallow arrived on the moon as a young dancer in 2862. She found lunar stage drama plagued by clumsy physics, where tragic deaths looked like slow floating. Sallow spent ten years in the low-gravity gymnasiums of the southern dome, training her spine to resist the theatre-drafts.

In her 2890 debut as Juliet, her final collapse took nine minutes. She did not use wires. Audiences, accustomed to the fast drop of Earth plays, watched her knees bend for three minutes before her waist followed.

By 2910, Sallow had perfected the forty-five-minute faint. During a performance of *The Glass Gasket*, she began her fall at eight o'clock. The theatre ran out of tissue by the half-hour mark. Her head touched the floorboards exactly at the curtain bell.

She lived her final years quietly. Sallow is survived by her daughter, three stage-hands, and twelve leg-weights. Her funeral will be held on Friday. It is expected to last four days.
drafts.premise: Obituary: Madame Clara Sallow, 102, who revolutionised lunar theatre by perfecting a low-gravity tragic faint so excruciatingly slow that audiences wept for forty-five minutes before her head reached the floor.

drafts.headline: Art Movement Boycotting Blue Dissolves
drafts.body:
An elderly paint-grinder has died in Copernicus, ending the Society of Grey Realists.

The movement began in 2844. Three plasterers watched an Earthrise and found the blue oceans emotionally ostentatious. They vowed to paint only what was honest. They used local basalt dust, raw oil, and three flat brushes. Each painter spent six hours a day grinding rock with three iron pestles and a single shared pair of goggles. They worked in a basement room with four stools and no windows.

Rules were strict. Any member who looked at the home planet for more than three seconds paid a fine of two water-vouchers. By 2890, the society had twelve members, one easel, and forty-two paintings of the same gravel pile. They held one public exhibition, attracting seven visitors and a local dog.

The end began when a pipeline leak introduced blue copper salts to the basement floor. The artists refused to touch the stained concrete, sitting in silence for seven weeks before voting to disband.

"Earth was showing off," Al-Jamil said in his final broadcast. "Nobody needs that much water."
drafts.premise: The domed settlement of Copernicus has laid to rest the Society of Grey Realists, a century-old painting movement that furiously boycotted the colour blue on the grounds that Earth was being emotionally ostentatious.

drafts.headline: Tycho Dome Mourns An Airlock Smudge
drafts.body:
A junior vacuum-sweeper wiped the Grimy Corner from Lock Seven on Thursday.

The smudge began in 2861. A pipeline fitter pressed an oily glove against the viewport to check the seal.

In 2884, the critic Linus Cho noticed the shape. Cho declared the grey crescent a masterpiece of municipal despair. He wrote three books on its texture, calling it the ultimate expression of human dust. By 2910, the council had redirected two commuter tubes so passengers could view the smear. It survived the Great Degreasing of 2921.

To preserve the work, the municipal arts board took extreme measures. They installed a nitrogen nozzle to deflect solar wind. They hired one guard. He had a metal stool, a plastic barrier, and a book of codes. He did not speak for nine years.

An automated cleaning drone ended the run. It used three sprays of solvent. The glass is now clear.

The Tycho Arts Trust has ordered a week of silence. On Friday, eighty-four residents stood in the low gravity of Lock Seven to lay grey synthetic flowers at the metal sill.
drafts.premise: The arts establishment of Tycho Dome has declared an official week of mourning for 'The Grimy Corner,' an accidental grease smudge on an airlock viewport that three generations of critics passionately defended as a masterpiece of municipal despair.
